statement: A 5 by 5 board has its centre square cut out. A straight strip of 3 squares is placed on the board along a row or a column, so that it covers exactly 3 squares of the board and does not lie over the hole. In how many different positions can the strip be placed?

choices.misconception: I took away the 3 positions in the middle row that cover the hole, but forgot the 3 in the middle column.
I thought only the strip centred on the hole is blocked, so I took away just 1 position in the middle row and 1 in the middle column.
I counted all the positions on a full board and forgot about the hole.
I thought a strip of 3 can start in 4 places along a row of 5, then took away 4 positions in the middle row and 4 in the middle column.

hints: Count the positions on a board with no hole first.
On a full board, slide the strip along one row to count its positions, then use all the rows and columns. Then find which of those positions cover the centre square.
On a full board there are 3 positions in each row and each column, 30 in all. In the middle row every one of the 3 positions covers the centre square, and the same is true in the middle column.

solutions.reliable: First ignore the hole. In one row of 5 squares the strip can cover squares 1 to 3, 2 to 4 or 3 to 5, so 5 - 3 + 1 = 3 positions, and 5 rows give 15. The columns give another 15, so 30 in all. Now remove the positions that cover the centre square. It is square 3 of the middle row, and all three positions in that row include square 3. The same holds for the middle column. No other position covers the centre, so 30 - 3 - 3 = 24 positions remain. The transferable idea: count the easy whole first, then subtract exactly the cases that break the rule.
solutions.elegant: Count directly. The 4 rows without the hole have 3 positions each, 12 in all, and the middle row has none, because every block of 3 squares in a row of 5 includes the middle square. The columns give the same 12, so there are 24 positions.

whyOnTest: Counting by position with a twist: slide a window to count, then remove the blocked cases, noticing that every window in the middle line is blocked.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
